title: Product quantization II: asymmetric distance
summary: Precomputing an m by 256 table once per query turns scoring into table lookups and adds with no decode, and it is an exact reformulation rather than an approximation. Keeping the query unquantized is worth 17 points of recall over quantizing it, and the real win is 64 times less memory traffic.
html:
Yesterday ended on something clumsy. To score a query against a PQ code I reconstructed the approximate vector and took a dot product, which means decoding every candidate before I can reject it. Reconstructing a 384-dimension vector to find out it is irrelevant is a lot of work for a no.

The fix is a reformulation, and the nice part is that it is exact. You are not approximating the decode, you are computing the same number a cheaper way.

Split the dot product

A PQ code says: subspace 0 uses centroid 7, subspace 1 uses centroid 203, and so on. So the reconstructed vector is just those centroids laid end to end. Which means the dot product splits:

q . reconstructed  =  q_0 . codebook[0][code[0]]
                   +  q_1 . codebook[1][code[1]]
                   +  ...
                   +  q_m . codebook[m][code[m]]

Every term is a dot product between a slice of the query and one of 256 known centroids. The query does not change across candidates. The centroids do not change at all. Only the choice of which centroid changes.

So compute all of them up front, once per query:

table[j][c] = q_j . codebook[j][c]       for j in 0..m, c in 0..255

score(code) = sum over j of table[j][code[j]]

Scoring a candidate is now m table lookups and m adds. No decode, no multiplication, nothing touched but the m bytes of the code itself.

I checked this against decoding directly:

decode then dot:  0.01205683
ADC table sum  :  0.01205683
difference     :  2.79e-09

Floating point noise. Same number, different route.

Be precise about what is exact, though. ADC computes q . reconstructed(x) exactly. It does not compute q . x. All the error lives in the reconstruction, which is yesterday's lesson, and none of it comes from the lookup scheme. That matters because it tells you where to spend effort: raising m or improving the codebooks helps, and nothing about the scoring method does, because the scoring method is already exact for what it is scoring.

Why "asymmetric"

There is another way to do this. Quantize the query as well, then every comparison is centroid against centroid, and you can precompute a 256 by 256 table per subspace once at build time and never touch it again. That is symmetric distance computation, and it is tempting because the per-query setup disappears.

It is also worse, and the reason is simple. The query arrives exact. Keeping it exact costs nothing. Quantizing it throws away information you already had, in exchange for avoiding a setup step that is cheap anyway.

Measured, same codes, same corpus, m=24:

exact float32                   recall@10  1.000
ADC  (query kept exact)         recall@10  0.628
SDC  (query quantized too)      recall@10  0.457

Seventeen points of recall, given away for nothing. ADC is the one everyone uses, and this is why.

What it costs

full precision, per candidate :  384 multiply-adds,  1536 bytes read
ADC, per candidate            :   24 lookups + adds,   24 bytes read

ADC table build, once/query   :  256 x 384 = 98,304 multiply-adds

The table is not free, so there is a break-even. You spend 98,304 operations up front to save 360 per candidate, which pays off past 273 candidates. Below that, just use the full vectors. Above it, and any real index is scanning thousands, the table is noise.

Now the part that matters more than the operation count. Day 15 established that this is a bandwidth problem, not an arithmetic one, so look at bytes:

  1,000 candidates:  full    1.5 MB   ADC   0.024 MB
100,000 candidates:  full  153.6 MB   ADC   2.400 MB
1,000,000 candidates: full 1536.0 MB  ADC  24.000 MB     64x less, every time

Sixty four times less data crossing the memory bus. On a kernel that was memory bound by a factor of eight, that is the whole game, and it is why PQ speeds things up far more than the 16x reduction in arithmetic would suggest.

One more detail that makes it work in practice. The lookup table for m=24 is 24 times 256 floats, which is 24 KB. That fits in L1 cache on most CPUs and certainly in L2. So the table lookups are not memory accesses in any meaningful sense, they are a handful of cycles each against cache-resident data, while the thing you stream from RAM is a 24 byte code. You have arranged for the large, repeated reads to be tiny and the expensive data to be hot.

Where the fast implementations go from here

Once you see that the table is the hot structure, an obvious question follows: how small can it get? If 24 KB fits in L1, what fits in a register?

That is the idea behind the fast-scan family of implementations. Drop to 4 bit codes, so k=16 instead of 256, and a subspace table is 16 entries. Sixteen bytes of quantized values fit in a single SIMD register, and the lookup stops being a memory access at all: it becomes a byte shuffle instruction, which does sixteen lookups in one cycle with no load.

You give up codebook resolution, 16 centroids per subspace instead of 256, and you buy it back by using more subquantizers. The result is a scan that runs several times faster than the byte-code version while reading roughly the same number of bytes. It is the same reasoning chain all over again, just one level further down the memory hierarchy, and it is worth knowing about because the libraries you will actually use have it switched on.

An honest note on my timings

I measured ADC at 1.3 ms per query against 0.025 ms for exact numpy, which makes ADC look thirty times slower. That is real and it is an artefact. Exact search here is one BLAS matrix multiply over 6,200 vectors, hand-tuned assembly on contiguous memory. My ADC is a Python loop doing fancy indexing, and 6,200 candidates is below the break-even anyway.

The operation and bandwidth counts above are what transfers, because they are properties of the algorithm rather than of my implementation. In a real index, SIMD gathers do sixteen table lookups at once and the comparison runs the other way. If you benchmark this yourself in Python, expect the same disappointing result and do not conclude anything from it.

Where this leaves you

A billion vectors is 1.54 TB at full precision and 24 GB as PQ codes. The per-query table is 24 KB rebuilt each time. You can now scan compressed vectors at a fraction of the bandwidth, which solves the size problem, and Day 20 solved the which-vectors-to-look-at problem.

Nothing so far combines them. Tomorrow does: IVF-PQ, cells to decide where to look and codes to make looking cheap, which is the configuration that puts a billion vectors on a single machine.
exercise:
1. Verify the exactness claim. Take one query and one PQ code. Compute the score by decoding to a full vector and taking a dot product, then by building the m by 256 table and summing m lookups. The two numbers should agree to floating point noise. If they do not, your subvector slicing and your codebook indexing disagree somewhere.

2. Find your own break-even. For your dimension and your chosen m, compute 256 * d for the table and d - m saved per candidate, then divide. That candidate count is the point below which ADC is not worth doing. Compare it against how many candidates your nprobe setting from Day 20 actually produces.

3. Check the table fits in cache. Compute m * 256 * 4 bytes for a few values of m, and compare against your CPU's L1 and L2 sizes. Find the m where the table stops being L1 resident. That is a real ceiling on m that has nothing to do with recall, and it is the kind of constraint that only shows up when you think about where the data physically is.
